claim: Monitoring neuronal activity at single-cell resolution in freely moving Drosophila engaged in social behaviors is challenging because of their small size and lack of transparency.
source: Monitoring neuronal activity at single-cell resolution in freely moving Drosophila engaged in social behaviors is challenging because of their small size and lack of transparency.
evidence: This is a statement about the technical challenges of imaging in Drosophila, drawing from established knowledge in the field.

claim: Extant methods, such as Flyception, are highly invasive.
source: Extant methods, such as Flyception, are highly invasive.

claim: The study performs brain-wide mapping of active cells expressing the Immediate Early Gene hr38 using a high-sensitivity/low background fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) amplification method called HCR-3.0.

claim: P1a cells are an intensively studied population of male-specific interneurons.

claim: The study uses HI-FISH in combination with optogenetic activation of aggression-promoting neurons (opto-HI-FISH) to identify candidate downstream functional targets of these cells in a brain-wide, unbiased manner.
source: Using HI-FISH in combination with optogenetic activation of aggression-promoting neurons (opto-HI-FISH), we identify candidate downstream functional targets of these cells in a brain-wide, unbiased manner.
evidence: This describes a methodological approach and its application in the study.

claim: The study compares the activity of P1a neurons during sequential performance of courtship and aggression, using intronic vs. exonic hr38 probes to differentiate newly synthesized nuclear transcripts from cytoplasmic transcripts synthesized at an earlier time.

source: More recently, this method has been combined with tissue-clearing and light-sheet microscopy to perform systematic and unbiased whole-brain mapping of neurons activated during different behaviors (Kim et al., 2015; Renier et al., 2016).

claim: The study applied an ISH amplification technique called the hybridization chain reaction (HCR), v.3.0 to visualize the expression of Hr38.
source: To circumvent these problems, we have applied in this study an ISH amplification technique called the hybridization chain reaction (HCR), v.3.0 (Choi et al., 2018) to visualize the expression of Hr38, an IEG expressed by active neurons in the adult male fly brain (Fujita et al., 2013).

claim: Hr38 is an IEG expressed by active neurons in the adult male fly brain.
source: To circumvent these problems, we have applied in this study an ISH amplification technique called the hybridization chain reaction (HCR), v.3.0 (Choi et al., 2018) to visualize the expression of Hr38, an IEG expressed by active neurons in the adult male fly brain (Fujita et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The design of HCR requires conjoint hybridization to target sequences of adjacent pairs of 'half-probes' to achieve amplification.
source: The design of HCR, which requires conjoint hybridization to target sequences of adjacent pairs of 'half-probes' to achieve amplification, affords both greater sensitivity and specificity, allowing detection of low-abundance transcripts with minimal background noise and off-target hybridization.

claim: HCR affords both greater sensitivity and specificity, allowing detection of low-abundance transcripts with minimal background noise and off-target hybridization.
source: The design of HCR, which requires conjoint hybridization to target sequences of adjacent pairs of 'half-probes' to achieve amplification, affords both greater sensitivity and specificity, allowing detection of low-abundance transcripts with minimal background noise and off-target hybridization.

claim: The study calls the approach HCR3.0-amplified IEG Fluorescent In Situ Hybridization, or 'HI-FISH'.
source: We call this approach HCR3.0-amplified IEG Fluorescent In Situ Hybridization, or 'HI-FISH' (Figure 1A).

claim: The HI-FISH approach is in principle applicable to any IEG.
source: Although we use Hr38 as proof-of-concept, this approach is in principle applicable to any IEG.
evidence: This is a statement about the generalizability of the method.

claim: The HCR3.0 method provides greater sensitivity, specificity, and lower background than traditional FISH using Tyramide signal amplification.
source: The HCR3.0 method provides greater sensitivity, specificity, and lower background than traditional FISH using Tyramide signal amplification.
evidence: This is a comparison of HCR3.0 to traditional methods.

claim: Application of older FISH methods in the Drosophila adult whole brain has been limited, due to low sensitivity and high background.
source: Application of older FISH methods in the Drosophila adult whole brain has been limited, due to low sensitivity and high background (Wilkie and Davis, 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Application of the HCR-FISH method was able to detect mRNA encoding an octopamine receptor Oct-TyrR.
source: Application of the HCR-FISH method, by contrast, was able to detect mRNA encoding an octopamine receptor Oct-TyrR (Arakawa et al., 1990; Saudou et al., 1990), as well as Dh44, a high-abundance neuropeptide-encoding transcript (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B; Choi et al., 2018).

claim: Application of the HCR-FISH method was able to detect Dh44, a high-abundance neuropeptide-encoding transcript.
source: Application of the HCR-FISH method, by contrast, was able to detect mRNA encoding an octopamine receptor Oct-TyrR (Arakawa et al., 1990; Saudou et al., 1990), as well as Dh44, a high-abundance neuropeptide-encoding transcript (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B; Choi et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B and citations.

claim: Background in controls lacking the HCR initiator probes was essentially undetectable.
source: Background in controls lacking the HCR initiator probes was essentially undetectable.

claim: Following photostimulation of Fru-GAL4 neurons, Hr38 signals were detected in virtually all Chrimson::tdT+ neurons as well as in other tdT− neurons.
source: Following photostimulation, Hr38 signals were detected in virtually all Chrimson::tdT+ neurons as well as in other tdT− neurons (Figure 1B, C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1B, C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: tdT− neurons that express Hr38 after photostimulation of Fru-GAL4 neurons may be indirectly activated via synaptic inputs from Fru-GAL4+ neurons.
source: The latter may be indirectly activated via synaptic inputs from Fru-GAL4+ neurons.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism of Hr38 induction in tdT− neurons.

claim: Control flies of the same genotype but without photostimulation displayed much lower levels of Hr38 expression.
source: Control flies of the same genotype but without photostimulation, or photostimulated flies with an 'empty' GAL4 driver (BDPG4uw; Pfeiffer et al., 2008) displayed much lower levels of Hr38 expression.
evidence: This statement is supported by data comparing experimental and control conditions.

claim: Photostimulated flies with an 'empty' GAL4 driver (BDPG4uw) displayed much lower levels of Hr38 expression.
source: Control flies of the same genotype but without photostimulation, or photostimulated flies with an 'empty' GAL4 driver (BDPG4uw; Pfeiffer et al., 2008) displayed much lower levels of Hr38 expression.
evidence: This statement is supported by data comparing experimental and control conditions, with a citation for the GAL4 driver.

claim: Simply transferring flies to a new arena induced a significant level of Hr38 expression throughout the brain.
source: While performing these experiments, we observed that simply transferring flies to a new arena induced a significant level of Hr38 expression throughout the brain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E), likely reflecting the stress caused by the manipulation and new environment.
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: Hr38 expression induced by transferring flies to a new arena likely reflects the stress caused by the manipulation and new environment.
source: While performing these experiments, we observed that simply transferring flies to a new arena induced a significant level of Hr38 expression throughout the brain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E), likely reflecting the stress caused by the manipulation and new environment.
evidence: This is an inference about the cause of Hr38 induction.

claim: Habituation of flies to the testing arena before starting the assays proved essential to distinguishing behavior-specific HI-FISH signals from the widespread Hr38 induction caused by transfer of the flies from their home vial to an experimental apparatus.
source: This minor modification proved essential to distinguishing behavior-specific HI-FISH signals from the widespread Hr38 induction caused by transfer of the flies from their home vial to an experimental apparatus.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of the habituation procedure based on experimental observations.

claim: P1a neurons were initially identified in functional screens for aggression-promoting neurons.
source: As an initial proof-of-concept application of HI-FISH, we asked whether neuronal subsets initially identified in functional screens for aggression-promoting neurons (Asahina et al., 2014; Hoopfer et al., 2015; Watanabe et al., 2017) were actually active during natural aggressive behavior.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Tachykinin-FruM+ (TkFruM) neurons were initially identified in functional screens for aggression-promoting neurons.
source: These included P1a (Hoopfer et al., 2015), Tachykinin-FruM+ (TkFruM) (Asahina et al., 2014), and aSP2 neurons (Watanabe et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: aSP2 neurons were initially identified in functional screens for aggression-promoting neurons.
source: These included P1a (Hoopfer et al., 2015), Tachykinin-FruM+ (TkFruM) (Asahina et al., 2014), and aSP2 neurons (Watanabe et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Activity in P1a, TkFruM, and aSP2 neurons was shown to be essential for normal aggression.
source: Despite the fact that activity in these neuron subsets was shown to be essential for normal aggression, it was formally possible that the behavioral phenotypes caused by their artificial stimulation were due to their supra-physiological activation.
evidence: This statement is based on prior functional studies cited earlier.

claim: In the control condition, where the experimental flies were kept alone during the observation period, there was little or no detectable Hr38 expression in P1a, Tk, or aSP2 neurons.
source: In the control condition, where the experimental flies were kept alone during the observation period, there was little or no detectable Hr38 expression in P1a, Tk, or aSP2 neurons (Figure 2A–D, 'Control').

source: In contrast, we observed clear Hr38 signals in GFP+ P1a, Tk, and aSP2 neurons after a male–male interaction that included fighting behavior (Aggression: Figure 2A–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2A–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: P1a-negative Hr38+ neurons neighboring P1a neurons were observed during aggression.
source: We also observed P1a-negative Hr38+ neurons neighboring P1a neurons during aggression (Figure 2, P1a Hr38).

source: These cells may correspond to other subpopulations of P1 neurons, or to Dsx-expressing pC1 neurons that have also been implicated in aggression (Koganezawa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference about the identity of the Hr38+ neurons, with a citation to prior work on pC1 neurons.

claim: In the case of courtship with a female, comparably strong Hr38 induction was observed in P1a and aSP2 neurons.

evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2A–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no Hr38 expression in Tk neurons during courtship with a female.
source: In the case of courtship with a female, comparably strong Hr38 induction was observed in P1a and aSP2 neurons, while there was no Hr38 expression in Tk neurons (Figure 2A–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Courtship).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2A–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Hr38 expression data are consistent with prior observations indicating that the functional manipulation of P1a or aSP2 neurons in the male flies affects both male–male aggression and male–female courtship behavior.
source: These data are consistent with prior observations indicating that the functional manipulation of P1a or aSP2 neurons in the male flies affects both male–male aggression and male–female courtship behavior (Hoopfer et al., 2015; Takayanagi-Kiya and Kiya, 2019; Watanabe et al., 2017), while the manipulation of Tk neurons affects only aggression (Asahina et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement compares the current data to prior functional studies, supported by citations.

claim: The manipulation of Tk neurons affects only aggression.
source: These data are consistent with prior observations indicating that the functional manipulation of P1a or aSP2 neurons in the male flies affects both male–male aggression and male–female courtship behavior (Hoopfer et al., 2015; Takayanagi-Kiya and Kiya, 2019; Watanabe et al., 2017), while the manipulation of Tk neurons affects only aggression (Asahina et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Social interactions in flies consist of multiple phases: approach, investigation, initial contact, and progression to consummatory behaviors.
source: Social interactions in flies consist of multiple phases: approach, investigation, initial contact, and progression to consummatory behaviors (Chiu et al., 2021; Yamamoto and Koganezawa, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The detection of Hr38 (or any IEG) induction may reflect activation at any or all of the sequential phases of social behavior due to the long-lived, accumulated expression of the IEG mRNA.
source: While electrophysiological recording or calcium imaging can identify neuronal activation that is time-locked to specific behavioral actions, the detection of Hr38 (or any IEG) induction may reflect activation at any or all of these sequential phases due to the long-lived, accumulated expression of the IEG mRNA.
evidence: This is a statement about the temporal limitations of IEG-based methods.

claim: The fraction of Hr38+ cells among P1a, Tk, and aSP2 neurons in the 'dead male' condition was slightly lower but not statistically significantly different from that measured during actual aggression.
source: In both 'touching but no fighting' conditions, the fraction of Hr38+ cells among P1a, Tk, and aSP2 neurons was slightly lower but not statistically significantly different from that measured during actual aggression, while the intensity of Hr38 mRNA expression in positive cells was slightly lower in the No Food condition (Dead Male and No Food: Figure 2B–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2B–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The intensity of Hr38 mRNA expression in positive cells was slightly lower in the No Food condition.
source: In both 'touching but no fighting' conditions, the fraction of Hr38+ cells among P1a, Tk, and aSP2 neurons was slightly lower but not statistically significantly different from that measured during actual aggression, while the intensity of Hr38 mRNA expression in positive cells was slightly lower in the No Food condition (Dead Male and No Food: Figure 2B–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2B–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The activation of P1a, Tk, or aSP2 neurons does not require consummatory aggressive actions such as lunging, tussling, or boxing.
source: Thus the activation of P1a, Tk, or aSP2 neurons does not require consummatory aggressive actions such as lunging, tussling, or boxing (Chen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data comparing fighting and non-fighting conditions, with a citation for the aggressive behaviors.

claim: Inter-male aggression has been shown to require both detection of volatile cues by the olfactory system, and of non-volatile cues by the gustatory system.
source: In the case of chemosensory signals, inter-male aggression has been shown to require both detection of volatile cues by the olfactory system, and of non-volatile cues by the gustatory system (Fernández and Kravitz, 2013; Wang et al., 2011; Wang and Anderson, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The detection of non-volatile cues requires contact chemosensation.
source: While both types of cues are present when an experimental fly is exposed to an intact or a dead male fly, the detection of non-volatile cues requires contact chemosensation (Vosshall and Stocker, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Hr38 induction in all three cell populations (P1a, Tk, aSP2) under the mesh condition was significantly weaker than that measured during free interaction with a male on agarose, where contact but no fighting occurred.
source: Interestingly, Hr38 induction in all three cell populations under this condition was significantly weaker than that measured during free interaction with a male on agarose, where contact but no fighting occurred (Mesh: Figure 2B–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2B–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Strong activation of P1a, Tk, and aSP2 neurons requires the integration of both volatile and non-volatile male-derived chemosensory cues.
source: Taken together with the relatively strong Hr38 induction observed following contact with a dead male (which presumably provides a source of both olfactory and gustatory pheromones), these data suggest that strong activation of P1a, Tk, and aSP2 neurons requires the integration of both volatile and non-volatile male-derived chemosensory cues.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data comparing different sensory conditions.

claim: The results do not exclude the possibility that P1a, Tk, and aSP2 neurons exhibit additional activity during contact-mediated aggression, but which is not statistically detectable by this method in comparison to 'no fighting' controls.
source: However, the results do not exclude the possibility that these neurons exhibit additional activity during contact-mediated aggression, but which is not statistically detectable by this method in comparison to 'no fighting' controls.
evidence: This is a caveat about the interpretation of the data.

claim: Optogenetic and thermogenetic stimulation experiments have shown that P1a interneurons can promote both male-directed aggression and male- or female-directed courtship.
source: Optogenetic and thermogenetic stimulation experiments have shown that P1a interneurons can promote both male-directed aggression and male- or female-directed courtship (Hoopfer et al., 2015; von Philipsborn et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The neural circuitry downstream of P1 neurons that promotes female-directed courtship behavior has been well-characterized.
source: While the neural circuitry downstream of P1 neurons that promotes female-directed courtship behavior has been well-characterized (von Philipsborn et al., 2011), the pathway by which P1a neurons can promote aggression is poorly understood.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The pathway by which P1a neurons can promote aggression is poorly understood.
source: While the neural circuitry downstream of P1 neurons that promotes female-directed courtship behavior has been well-characterized (von Philipsborn et al., 2011), the pathway by which P1a neurons can promote aggression is poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Neurons around the posterior dorsal region of the central brain were strongly activated by P1a stimulation.
source: The heat map indicated that neurons around the posterior dorsal region of the central brain were strongly activated by P1a stimulation (Figure 3F).

claim: pCd neurons were previously shown by calcium imaging to be (indirect) targets of P1a neurons.

claim: Hr38 was strongly induced in pCd neurons by P1a photostimulation.

claim: Evidence of Hr38 induction was observed in Kenyon cells (KCs) following P1a optogenetic activation.

claim: Evidence of Hr38 induction was observed in PAM dopaminergic neurons following P1a optogenetic activation.
source: We observed evidence of Hr38 induction in all three cell populations, although the signal was difficult to quantify due to the high density of GFP+ cells (Figure 3G).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The neurites of both KCs and PAM neurons showed significant time-locked responses to optogenetic activation of P1a neurons.
source: The neurites of both KCs and PAM neurons showed significant time-locked responses to optogenetic activation of P1a neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–F.

claim: Clear responses were observed in cell bodies of PAM neurons during P1a photostimulation.
source: We also imaged jGCaMP7b signals from cell bodies of PAM neurons while photostimulating P1a neurons, and observed clear responses in both cases as well (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–J).
evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–J.

claim: P1a photostimulation evoked a significant rise in ∆F/F in~50% of PAM neurons.

evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1I.

claim: The opto-HI-FISH data validate the results from brain-wide Hr38 induction mapping.
source: These data validate the results from brain-wide Hr38 induction mapping and provide proof-of-concept that brain regions containing functional targets of a cell population of interest (here P1a neurons), as well as specific neuron subtype targets within these regions (KCs and PAM neurons), can be identified by opto-HI-FISH.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of opto-HI-FISH and calcium imaging data.

claim: Brain regions containing functional targets of a cell population of interest, as well as specific neuron subtype targets within these regions, can be identified by opto-HI-FISH.
source: These data validate the results from brain-wide Hr38 induction mapping and provide proof-of-concept that brain regions containing functional targets of a cell population of interest (here P1a neurons), as well as specific neuron subtype targets within these regions (KCs and PAM neurons), can be identified by opto-HI-FISH.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of the opto-HI-FISH method.

claim: The opto-HI-FISH results are consistent with a recent report showing that subsets of PAM dopaminergic neurons receive excitatory inputs from P1 neurons, and assign to KCs a positive valence associated with P1 activation.
source: These results are also consistent with a recent report showing that subsets of PAM dopaminergic neurons receive excitatory inputs from P1 neurons, and assign to KCs a positive valence associated with P1 activation (Shen et al., 2023).

claim: Previous reports showed that artificial activation of P1a neurons promoted both aggression and courtship.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of HI-FISH based on the data presented.

claim: HI-FISH can be used to identify candidate downstream targets of neurons following their optogenetic activation (opto-HI-FISH).
